Twyla Tharp is an American dancer and choreographer who seamlessly blended contemporary dance, ballet, and popular culture, creating a movement vocabulary that is both athletic and emotionally direct. Her prolific output and fearless genre-hopping from concert dance to Broadway to film established her as one of the most innovative choreographers of the late twentieth century. Born in nineteen forty-one in Indiana, she studied ballet, tap, jazz, and modern dance, synthesizing these vocabularies into a distinctly American style. She formed the Twyla Tharp Dance Company in nineteen sixty-five and created over one hundred thirty works that ranged from pure-dance abstractions to narrative pieces with popular music. She collaborated extensively with Mikhail Baryshnikov, including the groundbreaking Push Comes to Shove in nineteen seventy-six, which introduced ballet audiences to postmodern movement. She created Hair in nineteen eighty-seven, Singin' in the Rain in nineteen eighty-five, and Movin' Out in two thousand two, each redefining how dance could work in theatrical contexts. She was known for using popular music including Billy Joel, Frank Sinatra, and David Byrne as equally valid material for dance, breaking the hierarchy between serious and entertainment art. She directed and choreographed films including Amadeus in nineteen eighty-four, White Nights in nineteen eighty-five, and Hair in nineteen seventy-nine, bringing dance to cinematic audiences. She published an influential memoir, Push Comes to Shove, and wrote extensively about dance process and creativity.
